conversation.content:
Good morning, I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Maya Bennett—I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician here at the women’s clinic. I specialize in the emotional changes that can happen during pregnancy and after birth, and I’m here simply to listen and help you feel supported.

We’re going to use a short questionnaire called the EPDS—Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s just ten questions about how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; it simply gives us a snapshot of how things are going for you right now so we can figure out the best way to support you.

Everything we talk about stays between us unless there’s an immediate safety concern, and you can skip anything that feels uncomfortable. We’ll take it one question at a time, and I’ll re-phrase each item so it feels more like a conversation than a checklist.

Ready to begin?

First, I’d love to know: in the past week, have you still been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

Honestly… it’s been hard. I can still chuckle if my partner does something silly or if the baby makes a goofy face, but it feels kind of forced—like I’m going through the motions. Most of the time I’m too tired or worried to find things genuinely funny the way I used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… I mean, I can manage a little laugh here or there, but it doesn’t feel natural or last long. Mostly I’m just too worn-out and on-edge to find much funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still try to plan little things—like taking the baby for a short walk or having my favorite coffee—but when the moment comes, it feels kind of flat. I tell myself I should be excited, yet the enjoyment is nowhere near what it used to be, and sometimes I just skip it because it feels like too much effort.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—maybe my milk isn’t good enough or I missed his sleepy cues. Even little stuff, like spilling a bottle or being late to change him, turns into this loop of “I’m a bad mom.” I know, rationally, it’s not all my fault, but the guilt just pops up before I can stop it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Most days, yeah. It’s like there’s this low-level hum of worry in the back of my head, even when everything looks fine—like I’ll suddenly picture the baby not breathing in the bassinet or worry that a car is going to run us down on our short walk. No real reason, just these flashes I can’t seem to switch off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes it spikes past worry into this sudden "can't-catch-my-breath" feeling—like last night, out of nowhere, my heart was racing and I was convinced something awful was about to happen, even though the baby and I were just sitting on the couch. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes. A lot of the time it feels like the dishes, the laundry, the feeds, the texts I haven’t answered—they’re all stacked up and I can’t see the top. I still push through because I have to care for him, but I’m running on empty and it feels like I’m barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I’ll lie down exhausted, but my brain won’t settle. I keep replaying everything I might have messed up that day or imagining scary “what-ifs” about the baby. It can take an hour or more to drift off, and then I wake up with my heart pounding at every little sound.
I have felt sad or miserable

That pretty much sums up most days. There’s this heavy, sad feeling that tags along from morning to night. It’s not tears every second, just this dull ache that makes everything feel gray and kind of hopeless.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a couple of times this week. Once when the baby wouldn’t settle and I felt like I was failing him, and another time when I caught sight of myself in the mirror and just felt like a stranger in my own body and life. The tears come fast, and once they start it’s hard to turn them off.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

A couple of fleeting thoughts have popped up—like wondering if everyone would be better off without me—but they’re quick and I haven’t made any plans or anything. Still, when they hit, it scares me that my mind even goes there.

You've shared that the past week has felt heavy and gray-laughing feels forced, activities you used to enjoy now seem flat, and a constant <sym>low-level worry</sym> or sudden <sym>panic</sym> leaves you exhausted. You describe blaming yourself for every hiccup with your baby, crying easily, struggling to fall and stay asleep, and feeling overwhelmed by everyday tasks. Occasional fleeting thoughts that loved ones might be better off without you frighten you, even though you have no intention of acting on them.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only brief, forced laughter, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient recognizes a clear reduction in anticipated enjoyment; activities feel "flat" and effortful, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame occurring "a lot," triggered by routine infant care, consistent with "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Persistent near-daily intrusive worries with vivid catastrophic imagery maps to "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic attacks with physical symptoms (racing heart, breathlessness, dread) that resolve quickly—semantically aligns with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling persistently overwhelmed by daily tasks and barely able to manage, matching 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty initiating sleep due to racing thoughts and frequent night waking, matching 'most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, daily sadness with a hopeless tone, aligning with 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes crying twice in the past week triggered by feeling overwhelmed and disconnected, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 24 places you well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable <med>postpartum depression</med> with <med>comorbid anxiety</med>. You endorse pervasive <sym>depressed mood</sym>, markedly diminished interest (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), <sym>insomnia</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, feelings of worthlessness/excessive guilt, and recurrent passive <sym>suicidal ideation</sym> (no plan), aligning with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Combined with near-daily <sym>anxiety</sym> and episodic <sym>panic symptoms</sym>, these findings warrant urgent evaluation and safety planning. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange an urgent same-week appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for full assessment and safety planning
2. Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department if <sym>self-harm thoughts</sym> become active or you feel unsafe
3. Ask a trusted adult to stay with you and help care for the baby while you seek treatment
4. Begin gentle daily structure: one small self-care task (shower, 5-minute porch break) and one pleasurable micro-activity; keep expectations minimal
5. Practice 4-7-8 breathing or progressive muscle relaxation when <sym>panic sensations</sym> arise; repeat 4 cycles
6. Limit information overload-mute non-essential social media and set a 15-minute news cap
7. Schedule a follow-up call with this office within 48 hours to confirm referral completion and safety
8. If breastfeeding, discuss medication options compatible with nursing during your consultation
9. Access local supports: postpartum support group, 24-hr Postpartum Support International warmline (1-800-944-4773, text 800-944-4773), and National Maternal Mental Health hotline (1-833-852-6262)
10. Continue attending scheduled pediatric visits so baby's well-being can be monitored alongside yours
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother (baby ≤ 1 yr) – self-report

A. Key Symptoms / Behaviors Endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, inability to laugh or feel enjoyment  
- Daily tearfulness and “heavy, hopeless” affect  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt (“bad mom” cognitions)  
- Difficulty falling/staying asleep related to rumination & worry  
- Chronic background anxiety with episodic panic symptoms (racing heart, breathlessness)  
- Sense of being overwhelmed and “running on empty”  
- Fleeting passive self-harm thoughts (“everyone better off without me”) – no plan or intent reported

B. Pattern Consistency  
Across all domains patient reports mood, anxiety, and coping difficulties that exceed typical postpartum adjustment; symptoms present most of the day, nearly every day, and interfere with daily functioning.

C. Screening Significance  
- Meets probable threshold for Major Depressive Episode (DSM-5) with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety features  
- Suicidal ideation present (passive) → elevated safety risk

D. Risk Factors Highlighted  
- Anhedonia, pervasive sadness, crying spells  
- Sleep disruption secondary to mood (not just infant care)  
- Heightened anxiety/panic attacks  
- Worthlessness/guilt out of proportion to events  
- Passive SI → warrants immediate safety assessment

E. Clinical Impression (Screening Only)  
High likelihood of clinically significant postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety. Passive suicidal ideation endorsed; safety evaluation and follow-up indicated. Recommend expedited referral for comprehensive mental health assessment and safety planning.
